Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Nalini had always enjoyed her job as a delivery driver, navigating the city streets with ease and chatting with customers along the way. But that all changed one fateful evening when she was mugged by a group of strangers while making a delivery in a quiet alleyway. The experience left her shaken, and over time, Nalini found herself increasingly unable to cope with the memories and emotions that lingered long after the event. As she recalled the incident, Nalini's mind would replay the sounds of her attackers' voices and the feeling of being trapped and helpless. These auditory flashbacks (Auditory Recall) were often accompanied by vivid snapshot memories (Snapshot Memory) of specific moments during the mugging, such as when one of the perpetrators grabbed her arm or when she saw a bystander walk away without intervening. The intensity of these memories would sometimes overwhelm Nalini, leaving her with a profound sense of emotion without any clear image or recollection (Emotion Without Image). Nalini's experiences had also left her with a deep-seated fear of being forced to do something against her will (Loss of Autonomy), which made encounters with authority figures like police officers particularly distressing (Authority Presence). When she saw people acting suspiciously (Perceived Threat) on the street, Nalini would immediately go on high alert, scanning her surroundings for potential escape routes (Escape Route Planning). At night, she would wake up multiple times to check whether she was safe (Waking Alert), unable to shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. As a result of these triggers and memories, Nalini began to develop maladaptive strategies to cope with her anxiety. She started avoiding driving or being a passenger in vehicles (Avoid Driving), which had been a source of joy for her before the mugging. On particularly difficult days, she would turn to substance use as a way to numb her emotions (Drug Use). Nalini also found herself engaging in magical thinking, telling herself that the event didn't really happen or wasn't that bad (Magical Thinking), as if trying to will away the trauma. However, these strategies only seemed to exacerbate Nalini's problems. Her avoidance of driving led to her losing her job and becoming increasingly isolated (Isolation). She began to feel like she was stuck in a cycle of guilt and self-blame (Inaction Guilt), unable to forgive herself for not doing more to stop the mugging. As time went on, Nalini became convinced that she was powerless to prevent bad things from happening to her (Helplessness). As her negative appraisals deepened, Nalini's world began to shrink further. She started to see potential threats everywhere, constantly scanning for danger and rehearsing worst-case scenarios in her mind. This sense of threat only served to reinforce her maladaptive strategies, as she became even more determined to avoid situations that might trigger memories or feelings of vulnerability. Nalini's memories continued to haunt her, with the sounds and images of the mugging replaying like a constant refrain in her mind. Her attempts to suppress these memories through magical thinking only seemed to make them more vivid and distressing. As she struggled to cope with her trauma, Nalini became increasingly aware that she needed help - but the thought of confronting her fears and emotions head-on was daunting. It wasn't until Nalini's friends and family staged an intervention, expressing concern about her escalating avoidance behaviors and self-destructive habits, that she finally sought professional help. With a mixture of trepidation and hope, Nalini took the first steps towards reclaiming her life from the grip of trauma - and slowly began to rebuild a sense of autonomy, purpose, and connection with others.
